entries.lesson_core_move: Express a periodic continuous-time signal in complex-exponential Fourier series form as a sum of integer-harmonic terms C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} with each coefficient weighting one harmonic.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex-Exponential Fourier Series Form

blocks.text: A periodic continuous-time signal can be written as a sum of complex exponentials at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.

In this notation, $C_k$ is the complex coefficient on the $k$th harmonic, $k$ is the integer label of that harmonic, and $\omega_0$ sets the spacing between harmonics. A simple starting picture is a signal with a DC term and one positive/negative harmonic pair.
Because $k$ runs over all integers, $k=0$ gives the DC term, while positive and negative values of $k$ give the matching $+k$ and $-k$ harmonic terms.
That grouped form makes the structure easy to read: $C_0$ stands alone, and each nonzero harmonic appears as a matched pair of complex exponentials with coefficients $C_k$ and $C_{-k}$.

Use this complex-exponential Fourier series form as the reusable template throughout the module: one coefficient per harmonic, one integer index per harmonic, and one fundamental frequency that sets the harmonic spacing.

sections.section_title: Writing a Periodic Signal as a Complex Harmonic Sum

example_content.example_prompt: Given the explicit harmonic terms $C_{-2} e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, $C_{-1} e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, $C_0$, $C_1 e^{j\omega_0 t}$, and $C_2 e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, write the signal in compact complex-exponential Fourier series form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is an explicit list of harmonic terms. Start by recognizing the DC term $C_0$ and the matching positive/negative harmonic pairs that already follow the $C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ pattern.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(t)=C_{-2} e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-1} e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_0+C_1 e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_2 e^{j2\omega_0 t}

explanation_blocks.text: Read $C_0$ as the $k=0$ contribution, then group the $k=1$ and $k=2$ pairs by their integer indices. The only change is the notation: the same harmonic content is being written in compact sum form.

This compact form says one coefficient weights one harmonic, and the integer index $k$ tells you which harmonic each coefficient belongs to. That is the reusable complex-exponential Fourier series form.

sections.section_title: Substituting the Fundamental Frequency into the Series Form

example_content.example_prompt: For a periodic signal with period $T_0=4$, substitute $\omega_0=\pi/2$ into $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the stated period $T_0=4$. That fixes the fundamental angular frequency at $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=\frac{\pi}{2}$, and the only new move is to replace $\omega_0$ with that value while keeping the harmonic pattern unchanged.
Now substitute $\omega_0=\pi/2$ everywhere it appears in the series. Leave the coefficient labels $C_k$ and the integer index range exactly as they are.

The structure is still the same complex-exponential Fourier series: one coefficient per harmonic, one integer index per harmonic, and the exponent now uses the concrete frequency $\pi/2$ instead of a symbolic $\omega_0$.

sections.section_title: Expanding the Sum into Indexed Harmonic Terms

example_content.example_prompt: Expand $\sum_{k=-2}^{2} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ into explicit harmonic terms.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the finite index range from $k=-2$ to $k=2$. Read that as the five harmonic indices $-2,-1,0,1,2$ and keep the coefficient/exponential pattern $C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ unchanged.
Substitute each integer value of $k$ into the same harmonic template. Write the negative-index terms first, include the $k=0$ DC term, and then continue with the positive-index terms in order.

The result makes the harmonic structure explicit: $C_0$ is the DC term, and the negative and positive harmonics appear as matched pairs around it. The index order matches the original bounds, so the expanded form still reflects the same series.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Coefficient Weight on a Harmonic Term

example_content.example_prompt: Given the term $C_{-3} e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$, identify the coefficient that weights that harmonic.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single harmonic term. Read the exponential first: $e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$ means the harmonic index is $k=-3$.
Match that index to the coefficient subscript. The weighting coefficient uses the same index and the same sign as the harmonic term.
So the coefficient that weights the term is $C_{-3}$, not the exponential term itself. The coefficient label is the reusable part to read from the series.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret each complex Fourier coefficient C_k as the magnitude-and-phase weight assigned to the kth complex-exponential harmonic in a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex Fourier Coefficients

blocks.text: Start with the complex Fourier series $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$. The coefficient on the $k$th exponential term is $C_k$, so the subscript tells you which harmonic the coefficient weights.

Use the simplest base case first: $x(t)=C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$. Here $C_1$ is the 1st-harmonic weight and $C_0$ is the DC weight, so one coefficient read already tells you which part of the signal each term controls.
Read each coefficient in polar form as $C_k=|C_k|e^{j\angle C_k}$. The magnitude $|C_k|$ gives the harmonic strength, and the phase $\angle C_k$ gives its offset.
A list of coefficients is therefore a compact description of the periodic signal: it tells you which harmonics are present and how strongly each one appears.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Harmonic Indexed by a Coefficient

example_content.example_prompt: In the term $C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, identify which harmonic $C_3$ weights and explain why the subscript, not the exponential alone, tells you the harmonic number.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient-subscript pair. In $C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, the subscript $3$ names the harmonic, so $C_3$ is the weight on the 3rd harmonic.
Read the subscript as the harmonic index $k=3$. That is the number you use to name the harmonic in words: the 3rd harmonic.
The exponential term agrees with that same index because the factor $e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ also carries the number $3$. The coefficient and the exponential are matched to the same harmonic.
So the answer is that $C_3$ weights the 3rd harmonic. The coefficient's value is not needed yet; this step is only about reading the harmonic index from the subscript.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Magnitude as Harmonic Weight

example_content.example_prompt: If $C_2=4e^{j\pi/6}$, state the weight of the 2nd harmonic and separate the magnitude from the phase.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the polar form of the coefficient. In $C_2=4e^{j\pi/6}$, the number in front of the exponential is the magnitude, so it is the weight of the 2nd harmonic.
Read the magnitude as $|C_2|=4$. That is the harmonic's strength or weight; the phase $\pi/6$ is separate and does not change that weight.
So the 2nd harmonic has weight 4, regardless of the phase. When the question asks for the harmonic's strength, report the magnitude and leave the angle out of the weight claim.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Phase as Harmonic Phase

example_content.example_prompt: If $C_{-1}=3e^{-j\pi/4}$, identify the phase of the $-1$st harmonic and keep it separate from the magnitude.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the polar form attached to the harmonic index. In $C_{-1}=3e^{-j\pi/4}$, the subscript $-1$ tells you which harmonic it is, and the angle $-\pi/4$ tells you the phase.
Read the angle as $\angle C_{-1}=-\pi/4$. That is the phase carried by the $-1$st harmonic.
The magnitude $3$ is separate. It tells you the harmonic's weight, but it does not change the phase.
So the phase answer is $-\pi/4$. When the question asks for phase, report the angle and leave the magnitude out of the claim.

sections.section_title: Reading Nonzero Coefficients as Present Harmonics

example_content.example_prompt: Given $C_{-2}=0$, $C_{-1}=2e^{j\pi/4}$, $C_0=3$, $C_1=0$, and $C_2=1e^{-j\pi/3}$, list the harmonics that are present in the signal and say which are absent.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient list. A harmonic is present exactly when its coefficient is nonzero, so the job is to keep the nonzero coefficients and drop the zeros.
Here $C_{-2}=0$ and $C_1=0$, so the $-2$nd harmonic and the 1st harmonic are absent. The nonzero coefficients are $C_{-1}=2e^{j\pi/4}$, $C_0=3$, and $C_2=1e^{-j\pi/3}$.
So the present harmonics are the $-1$st harmonic, the DC term at $k=0$, and the 2nd harmonic. The zero coefficients do not contribute to the signal.
That is the rule to use in this kind of question: nonzero coefficients mark present harmonics, and zero coefficients mark absent harmonics.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate complex Fourier coefficients by integrating x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t} over any one period and normalizing by the period to isolate the kth harmonic.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Coefficient Integral Over One Period

blocks.text: A periodic signal in complex-exponential Fourier series form is written with one coefficient per harmonic. Here $x(t)$ is the signal, $C_k$ is the coefficient, $k$ is the integer harmonic index, and $\omega_0$ is the fundamental angular frequency.

It is often helpful to read the same series as a DC term plus positive and negative harmonic pairs. The $k=0$ term is the DC component, and the nonzero indices appear symmetrically as matched positive and negative harmonics.

To isolate one coefficient $C_k$, multiply the signal by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$ and integrate over any interval of length $T_0$. The matching harmonic survives, while the other harmonics cancel over a full period.

That cancellation is orthogonality over one period: the matching exponential integrates to $1$, and every mismatched harmonic integrates to $0$. Because the signal repeats every $T_0$, the start time can be any $t_0$ as long as the interval length is $T_0$.
The working recipe is simple: choose $k$, multiply by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$, integrate across any one period, and divide by $T_0$. That gives the coefficient $C_k$ for the $k$th harmonic directly.

sections.section_title: Identifying T_0, omega_0, and k in the Coefficient Formula

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has $T_0=2$. Identify the coefficient formula for $C_3$ over the one-period interval $[-1,1]$ and state the corresponding $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the one-period interval $[-1,1]$. Its length is $2$, so $T_0=2$, and that means $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=\pi$.
The coefficient formula stays in normalized one-period form. For $C_3$, set $k=3$ and keep the matching exponential $e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$.
Substituting $T_0=2$ and $\omega_0=\pi$ gives the final setup on the stated interval. The integral is ready to use, but it is not evaluated yet.
This is the correct coefficient formula setup: identify the period, compute the fundamental frequency, choose the harmonic index, and write the normalized integral over one full period.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k from a Smooth Periodic Formula

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $C_2$ for $x(t)=2+3\cos(\pi t)-4\sin(2\pi t)$ over one period.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a smooth periodic sum with one DC term and two harmonics. For $C_2$, use the one-period coefficient formula with $T_0=2$ and the matching exponential $e^{-j2\pi t}$.
Rewrite the trigonometric terms in complex-exponential form so the target harmonic is visible. The only part that can match $k=2$ is the $e^{j2\pi t}$ contribution from the sine term.
After multiplying by $e^{-j2\pi t}$, every nonmatching exponential averages to zero over $[0,2]$. Only the constant term created by $2j\,e^{j2\pi t}$ survives the integral.
So the coefficient is $C_2=2j$. The pattern is: write the one-period integral, expose the matching exponential, and drop the orthogonal terms.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k Over a Shifted One-Period Interval

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $C_2$ for the same signal as in the previous example, but integrate over $[1,3]$ instead of $[0,2]$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same signal and the same harmonic, with only the one-period window shifted. The coefficient integrand is still one-period periodic, so moving the start of the interval does not change the average.
Because $f(t)$ has period $2$, the integral over any interval of length $2$ is the same. The shifted window $[1,3]$ therefore gives the same coefficient as the original one-period window $[0,2]$.
That is exactly the coefficient computed in the previous example, so the shifted interval does not change the result.
So the one-period coefficient is invariant under the interval shift: any length-$2$ integration window gives the same $C_2$.

sections.section_title: Splitting the Coefficient Integral Across Pieces of One Period

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $C_1$ for the piecewise periodic signal $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t<1$ and $x(t)=2$ on $1\le t<2$, with $T_0=2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a one-period signal whose formula changes at $t=1$. Split the coefficient integral at that boundary before simplifying anything.
Evaluate each piece separately. The two pieces share the same exponential factor, so the only difference is the constant multiplier and the endpoint values.
Now use $e^{-j\pi}=-1$ and $e^{-j2\pi}=1$ to simplify the endpoints. The two piecewise contributions combine into one coefficient.
So the coefficient is $C_1=-\frac{1}{j\pi}$. The procedure is the same for any piecewise signal: split at every boundary, integrate each piece, and then add the results.

sections.section_title: Checking That the Integral Isolates the kth Harmonic

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $C_2$ for $x(t)=1+2e^{j2\pi t}+7e^{j5\pi t}$ with $T_0=2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is already written as a sum of complex exponentials. For $C_2$, multiply by the matching kernel $e^{-j2\pi t}$ and look for the term that becomes constant.

explanation_blocks.latex: C_2=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^2 \bigl(1+2e^{j2\pi t}+7e^{j5\pi t}\bigr)e^{-j2\pi t}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^2 \bigl(e^{-j2\pi t}+2+7e^{j3\pi t}\bigr)\,dt

explanation_blocks.text: The DC term and the $k=5$ term are nonmatching exponentials. Over one full period, each integrates to zero, so only the constant $2$ survives.
That leaves only the matching harmonic. The coefficient integral is just the average of the constant term over the period.
So the integral isolates exactly the $k=2$ harmonic and returns its coefficient, $2$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC coefficient C_0 by setting k=0 in the complex Fourier coefficient integral and interpreting the result as the periodic signal's average value.

sections.section_title: Introduction to DC Coefficient as Average Value

blocks.text: The DC coefficient $C_0$ is the $k=0$ Fourier coefficient in the complex Fourier series. It is the constant term, so it represents the average level that remains after the oscillatory harmonics are removed.
To isolate $C_0$, set $k=0$ in that coefficient formula. That is the only change, and it tells you to look at the zero-frequency term rather than a nonzero harmonic.

Because the exponential factor becomes $1$, the coefficient integral simplifies to the average of $x(t)$ over one full period. The oscillatory weighting disappears, so only the period-average remains.
Any interval of length $T_0$ gives the same value, so the starting point $t_0$ can shift without changing $C_0$. The only requirement is that the integration interval span one complete period.
So $C_0$ is the DC level, or average value, of the periodic signal. The next examples will compute that average directly from the integral.

sections.section_title: Computing C_0 by Setting k=0 in the Coefficient Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $C_0$ for the periodic signal that equals $5$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $1$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$ by setting $k=0$ in the coefficient integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the $k=0$ coefficient, so start from the complex Fourier coefficient formula and remove the exponential weighting. For this example, use one full period on $0 \le t < T_0$ and compute the average value over that interval.
Set $k=0$ first, then split the period integral across the two constant pieces. Each piece contributes area, because $x(t)$ is constant on each subinterval.
Now evaluate the two areas: the first contributes $5 \cdot \frac{T_0}{4}$ and the second contributes $1 \cdot \frac{3T_0}{4}$. Add them, then divide by $T_0$ to get the average level.
So the DC coefficient is $C_0=2$. This is the constant average value of the signal over one period.

sections.section_title: Interpreting C_0 as the Average Value Over One Period

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal equals $4$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$, $1$ on $T_0/3 \le t < 2T_0/3$, and $0$ on $2T_0/3 \le t < T_0$. Compute $C_0$ and state the signal's average value.

explanation_blocks.text: The average value is the normalized one-period area, so compute the area of each constant piece and divide by $T_0$. The zero-height section still matters because it occupies part of the period, even though it contributes no area.
Now read each piece as a rectangle area: the first contributes $4\cdot \frac{T_0}{3}$, the second contributes $1\cdot \frac{T_0}{3}$, and the third contributes $0$. Add the areas before normalizing.
So the signal's average value is $\frac{5}{3}$. Because $C_0$ is the one-period average, the DC coefficient is also $C_0=\frac{5}{3}$.

sections.section_title: Choosing a Convenient Period for Computing C_0

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal with period $T_0=4$ is defined by $x(t)=3$ on $2 \le t < 4$ and $x(t)=1$ on $4 \le t < 6$, repeated periodically. Compute $C_0$ by integrating over the convenient one-period interval $[2,6]$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $C_0$ is a one-period average, so choose any interval of length $T_0=4$ that makes the pieces line up. Here $[2,6]$ is convenient because it matches the given breakpoints exactly.

On $[2,6]$, the signal is $3$ for length $2$ and $1$ for length $2$, so the integral is just the sum of two rectangle areas. No change of variables is needed because the chosen interval already matches the piecewise definition.
Now normalize the total area by the period length. The result is the same average value you would get from any other full period, because periodicity makes all one-period intervals equivalent.
So the convenient shifted interval gives $C_0=2$, and that is the signal's average value over one period.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero and Nonzero DC Coefficients from Signal Balance

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal equals $5$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $-1$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$. Determine whether $C_0$ is zero or nonzero and compute its value from the balance of positive and negative area.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the signed area balance, so compare the positive and negative contributions over one period before looking at the height alone. If the total signed area does not cancel, then $C_0$ is nonzero.

The positive piece contributes $5\cdot \frac{T_0}{4}$, while the negative piece contributes $-1\cdot \frac{3T_0}{4}$. The positive area is larger, so the cancellation is incomplete and the average stays above zero.
So $C_0$ is nonzero, and in fact $C_0=\frac{1}{2}$. The signal's average value is positive because its positive area outweighs its negative area over one period.

entries.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert between trigonometric and complex Fourier series forms by mapping the DC term and each sine-cosine harmonic pair to the corresponding positive- and negative-index complex coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Introduction to Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms

blocks.text: The trigonometric and complex Fourier series are two notations for the same periodic signal. Start with the simplest case: one DC term and one harmonic pair, so the coefficient mapping is easy to see before the full sum appears.
The DC term matches directly: $a_0/2$ in trigonometric form is $C_0$ in complex form. That is the base case for the whole conversion rule.

For each harmonic index $k \ge 1$, use Euler's identities to turn the cosine-sine pair into the positive and negative exponential pair. The forward map sends one trigonometric pair to two complex coefficients.
Going back the other way is just as direct. Add the pair to recover $a_k$, and subtract to recover $b_k$.

So the workflow is: match $a_0/2$ with $C_0$, then match each $a_k\cos(k\omega_0 t)+b_k\sin(k\omega_0 t)$ pair with $C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}+C_{-k}e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$. The next examples will apply the same mapping one harmonic at a time.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Mapping the DC Term Between Fourier Series Forms

example_content.example_prompt: If a trigonometric Fourier series has $a_0=18$, what is the corresponding complex DC coefficient $C_0$?

explanation_blocks.text: This is the simplest mapping: only the DC term changes, and no harmonic pair is involved. The cue is the constant term, which is $a_0/2$ in trigonometric form and $C_0$ in complex form.
Substitute the given value $a_0=18$ into the DC relationship. That gives the complex coefficient directly.
So the corresponding complex DC coefficient is $C_0=9$. The reverse check is immediate: doubling $C_0$ gives back $a_0=18$, so the signal itself has not changed.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Cosine Harmonic to Complex Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the cosine harmonic $x(t)=8\cos(3\omega_0 t)$ into its complex coefficient pair $(C_3,C_{-3})$.

explanation_blocks.text: A cosine-only harmonic is the cue. With no sine term, the complex pair must be real and symmetric, so the positive- and negative-index coefficients will match.
This rewrite isolates the two exponentials at $+3$ and $-3$. Reading off the coefficients gives the same value on both sides of the pair.
So the complex form of the cosine harmonic is $C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}+C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}=4e^{j3\omega_0 t}+4e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$. The signal is unchanged; only the representation has changed.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine Harmonic to Complex Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the sine harmonic $x(t)=6\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ into its complex coefficient pair $(C_2,C_{-2})$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a pure sine harmonic, so the complex pair must be purely imaginary with opposite signs. Rewrite the sine term in exponential form and match each exponential to its coefficient.

Now read off the coefficients term by term: the $e^{j2\omega_0 t}$ term gives $C_2=-3j$, and the $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$ term gives $C_{-2}=3j$. The two coefficients are conjugates with opposite signs, which is the sine pattern.
So the sine harmonic is represented by the same signal in complex form, with its content carried by a purely imaginary positive-negative coefficient pair.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine-Cosine Harmonic Pair to Complex Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $x(t)=4\cos(4\omega_0 t)+10\sin(4\omega_0 t)$ into its complex coefficient pair $(C_4,C_{-4})$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single harmonic index with both cosine and sine pieces. Use the cosine rule for the real part and the sine rule for the imaginary part, then combine them into one pair of complex coefficients.

explanation_blocks.latex: 4\cos(4\omega_0 t)+10\sin(4\omega_0 t)=2e^{j4\omega_0 t}+2e^{-j4\omega_0 t}-5j\,e^{j4\omega_0 t}+5j\,e^{-j4\omega_0 t}=(2-5j)e^{j4\omega_0 t}+(2+5j)e^{-j4\omega_0 t}

explanation_blocks.text: Now read off the two coefficients from the combined exponential form. The positive-index coefficient is $C_4=2-5j$, and the negative-index coefficient is $C_{-4}=2+5j$.
This mixed case shows the full pattern: the cosine part contributes the shared real value, and the sine part contributes opposite imaginary parts, producing a conjugate pair.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting Complex Coefficient Pairs Back to Sine and Cosine Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Given $C_5=1-3j$ and $C_{-5}=1+3j$, recover the trigonometric coefficients $a_5$ and $b_5$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a conjugate pair of complex coefficients. Use the reverse mapping formulas to recover the trigonometric coefficients from the real and imaginary parts.
So the trigonometric coefficients are $a_5=2$ and $b_5=6$. The same harmonic can therefore be written in trigonometric form as a cosine term plus a sine term.
This closes the mapping in the reverse direction: a conjugate complex pair gives back the matching sine-cosine coefficients for the same harmonic index.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret positive and negative harmonics as paired complex exponentials whose coefficients combine to represent each nonzero harmonic of a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Positive and Negative Harmonics

blocks.text: Read the complex Fourier series by integer harmonic index. $k=0$ is the DC term $C_0$, and every nonzero harmonic is read as a $+k$ / $-k$ pair.
Start with the simplest nonzero harmonic, $k=1$. Read $C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$ and $C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ as one paired contribution for the first harmonic.
The same pairing rule holds for every $k>0$. The positive and negative indices are two contributions to one nonzero harmonic, not two separate harmonics.
Keep $C_0$ separate as the unpaired DC term. That cleanly separates the DC component from all nonzero harmonics in later examples.

sections.section_title: Identifying Positive and Negative Harmonic Indices

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=C_0+C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, identify which term is DC, which term is positive index, and which term is negative index.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the signed harmonic index attached to each term. Read the sign on the index to decide whether the term is zero, positive, or negative.
$C_0$ is the zero-index DC term. $C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}$ is the $+2$ harmonic term, and $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$ is the $-2$ harmonic term.
So the signed indices are $0$, $+2$, and $-2$. The sign on the harmonic index, not the coefficient name alone, is what classifies each term.

sections.section_title: Matching the Positive and Negative Terms for the Same Harmonic

example_content.example_prompt: From the terms $C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$, $C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, $C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, and $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, match the positive and negative terms that belong to the same harmonic.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the absolute harmonic index. Terms match only when the magnitude is the same and the signs are opposite.

explanation_blocks.latex: C_1e^{j\omega_0 t},\qquad C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t},\qquad C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t},\qquad C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}

explanation_blocks.text: Match $C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$ with $C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, and match $C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}$ with $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$. Each pair uses the same harmonic number with opposite signs.
So the answer is two matched harmonic pairs: one pair for harmonic number $1$ and one pair for harmonic number $2$. Nothing else is left unpaired in this example.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Harmonic Pair as One Nonzero Frequency Component

example_content.example_prompt: Interpret the pair $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}+C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$ as one nonzero harmonic component and state what harmonic number it represents.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the matched $+4$ / $-4$ pair. Read the two terms together as one nonzero harmonic component, not as separate harmonics.
This is the $k=4$ harmonic, so the frequency magnitude is $4\omega_0$.
So the pair names one nonzero frequency component at $4\omega_0$, and the two coefficients together describe that single component.

sections.section_title: Separating Nonzero Harmonic Pairs from the DC Term

example_content.example_prompt: Separate the DC term from the nonzero harmonic pairs in $x(t)=C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unpaired $C_0$ term. Everything with a $+k$ / $-k$ index belongs to a nonzero harmonic pair, while $C_0$ is the zero-frequency DC term.
So isolate $C_0$ first, then group the $+1$ and $-1$ terms together and the $+2$ and $-2$ terms together.
That leaves one DC term and two nonzero harmonic pairs, one for $k=1$ and one for $k=2$. The DC term stays separate from every nonzero harmonic pair.
